_doc: RULINGS on the crosswalk's proposals. tools/read_land_sales.py --build folds this file onto resident_crosswalk.json; --check refuses a ruling that names a spelling the register does not hold, or a person the proposal did not name. This file is HAND-AUTHORED and is the one file under data/research/land_sales/ that is not derived from the deposit — a judgement is not a derivation, and the project does not pretend otherwise.
why_this_exists: build_resident_crosswalk() applies ONE mechanical rule: the surname agrees, the residents layer holds exactly one person of that surname, and the first forename agrees in full or as an initial. That rule proposes; it does not decide. tools/spend_land_sales.py's own rule 1 says so in as many words — 'ONLY WHAT THE CROSSWALK ALREADY DECLARED. This pass re-adjudicates nothing.' — so between the proposal and the card there was nobody. T-0700 is the ticket that noticed it, against the nine spellings the ring townships added (T-0676).
the_ruling_rule: A proposal is UPHELD only where the town's own record of the person carries something the register's row can be checked against BEYOND a bare name — a middle initial the register repeats, a trade the purchase is consistent with, a second document, or the register's own Residence column. Where the town holds nothing but a name read once off a post-office letter list, the proposal rests on the residents layer being THIN rather than on the two records agreeing: an uncalled-for letter says a correspondent thought the name reachable at Chicago, and a tract entry says a name entered ground, and two name-only readings do not make an identity. Such a proposal is REFUSED. A ruling never raises a grade, never mints a resident, and never asserts a residence; a refusal retracts what a pass had already written.
scope: The nine purchaser spellings the ring deposit (T-0676) added, ruled under T-0700; the twenty-six the first deposit matched, ruled under T-0850 — sixteen upheld, ten refused; and, under T-0990, COHORT A — the fourteen proposals whose crosswalk match is `initial_agrees` AND whose `rivals[]` is non-empty, which is where the mechanical rule is weakest: the layer holds a namesake of the surname and a forename INITIAL alone chose between them. Eleven upheld, three refused. What is left unruled is the rest of what T-0697 ADDED when the mechanical rule stopped requiring exactly one person of the surname; the count is on the crosswalk's own `ruled` block rather than in this sentence, and the next cohort is its own ticket.
ruled_by: the steward loop, under T-0700, T-0850 and T-0990

ruled.reasoning: The initial alone would not carry it. What carries it is that the SAME register spells him PEARSONS HIRAM on twenty-eight other rows, one of which states COOK, and that the seventeen H rows are one hand at work: sixteen of them fall on a single day, 26 June 1835, in one township, T39N R13E, and eight of those in one section. A speculator buying half of section 10 and all four eighths of section 14 in an afternoon is the man the town already holds buying at the ring, not a second Pearsons who happens to share the county, the month and the surname.

The middle initial is the check the bare-name rule lacks, and it agrees: the town's man is Walter LOOMIS Newberry, attested at the American of 1835 and in both Fergus directories, and the register writes WALTER L. Six ring tracts entered on 26 and 27 June 1835 sit beside the town lots he was trading in the same season. Nothing here says he lived on any of it.

The town's James Whitlock is documented in four numbers of the Democrat between March and July 1835 AT A TRADE, and the trade is register of the land office. A land-office register entering a federal tract in June 1835 is the purchase the record would predict; the two readings are consistent in occupation as well as in name, which is the corroboration the mechanical rule could not see. The trade is what upholds this, and it is not evidence that he lived on the eighty acres in T38N R14E.

The middle initial agrees — the register writes CAMPBELL JAMES B and the town holds James B Campbell — and the town holds him across nine sources, from the poll lists of 1833-1835 to the old-settler notices, which is the densest record of the nine. Two tracts on one day, 8 August 1835, in T38N R14E and T38N R15E.

The town's record is a single post-office letter list — the weakest it accepts — and by the ruling rule that alone would refuse. It does not, because the list did not print a bare name: the Democrat of 28 January 1834 prints 'David P.Frame' and the register writes FRAME DAVID P. All three tokens agree, and a middle initial is exactly the second discriminator T-0696 says the crosswalks want. Upheld on the initial, and on nothing else: the entry proposes no residence, and the identity remains inferred.

The register itself supplies the check. Of the two rows entering the south-east quarter of section 12, T40N R13E on 10 April 1835, ls0912 states the purchaser's Residence as COOK — so the source that names him also places him in Cook County that spring, and the town's 1835 poll list places a Frank Dill at Chicago in the same year. Two records, an uncommon forename, and the county agreeing between them. WHAT THE RULING ALSO FOUND: the crosswalk was grading this proposal `inferred` and printing `residence_column: UNKNOWN`, because build_resident_crosswalk read the residence off the FIRST row of a spelling and the first row is the UNKNOWN one. The README's own rule is that a COOK row grades `documented` for residence in Cook County on the date of sale. The generator now reads every row of a spelling, and this proposal grades documented for that and nothing more — Cook County in 1835 reaches far beyond the town, and no residence in Chicago is asserted here.

SPENCER WILLIAM G is refused against William Spencer: the town's whole record of that man is one line of a post-office letter list — 'Spencer, William' in the Democrat's return of uncalled-for letters of 1 July 1835 — with no trade, no street and no second document, and the register adds a middle initial G the town has never seen. The mechanical rule fired because the residents layer holds exactly one Spencer, which is a fact about how thin the layer is and not about the man. Two name-only readings, disagreeing on the one token that could discriminate them.

WILSON JOHN L is refused against John Wilson. The town's John Wilson is known from a single return of uncalled-for letters, the Democrat of 28 January 1834, and nothing else names him; the register adds a middle initial L the town has never seen; and John Wilson is the commonest name in this corpus, so the rule's premise — exactly one of the surname in the residents layer — measures the layer and not the population. The three entries are also of 26 January and 10 March 1836, half a year past the town's last sight of the name. Refused on the ruling rule, and it would be refused on the initial alone.

GARRETT A ET CO is refused against A. Garrett — not because the firm is a stranger, but because the purchaser is a FIRM and this crosswalk proposes correspondences between a purchaser and a PERSON. 'ET CO' is the register saying the buyer was a partnership; the eighty acres in T38N R14E entered on 1 December 1835 were entered by the house, and a card that says this person entered them says something the page does not. The town's A. Garrett is well attested — an auctioneer in four numbers of the American and the Democrat — and the identification of the firm with him is probably right and is not what is refused. Reading firms as entities in their own right, so a partnership's purchase can be recorded against the partnership and its partners named, is T-0851.

The spelling T-0700 ruled on was the initial one; this is the full one, and it carries what that ruling leaned on. Twenty-eight rows over three years and 1,157 acres, one of them stating COOK, and the town's card names the trade outright: Hiram Pearsons is a speculator on Andreas's own list and on the poll of 1834. A register recording a man of that name buying half the ground he could reach is the trade the card already asserts, doing what the card says it did. Upholding the full spelling and refusing the initial one would also be incoherent, since T-0700 upheld PEARSONS H precisely BECAUSE these twenty-eight rows exist.

One quarter-section, 18 June 1836, and the only Elston in 431 purchaser spellings; the residents layer holds one too. What carries it is not the rarity but the bracket: the man is an advertiser in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 and is still in the town for Fergus' directory of 1839, so the town's own record holds him on BOTH sides of the entry date rather than at one point near it. Nothing here says he lived on the tract or moved to it.

Two canal rows of 29 September 1830, one of them stating ILLINOIS. The date is the check. The town's own record bounds this man at Chicago by 31 December 1830 off the old-settler death notices, so the entry falls INSIDE the life the town holds rather than years to either side of it, and the ground he enters — the E2NE of section 9, which 18 standing roofs sit on — is the ground beside James Kinzie's E2NW of the same section entered the day before in the same sale. One agent's transaction on one day, and the town holds one Wolcott. What is NOT ruled is residence: a canal entry says a name took ground, and the ILLINOIS in the residence column is a state.

Thirteen parcels over the three days of the school-section auction, 22-24 October 1833, and the town's own tax list of 1833 names an Arthur Bronson in the same year. A town assessing a man and an auction of the town's own school section are the same twelve months and the same ground. The forename is also doing real work in this register rather than riding on a rare surname: BRONSON FREDERIC and BRONSON FREDERICK stand beside him on other rows, and the layer holds only the Arthur. The old-settler death notices are the second document.

The town's own poll list of 10 August 1833 and its tax list of 1833 both print Carver, David — two months before the school-section auction he buys at on 25 October 1833. Andreas gives him the trade, lumber merchant, and the register holds no other Carver. A townsman on the town's own rolls buying at the town's own sale, in the same season, is a correspondence with a date behind it and not merely a name.

The middle initial, printed on both sides. The register spells him CASEY EDWARD W; the town's tax list of 1833 and poll of 1834 both print 'Casey, Edward W.' This is the NEWBERRY WALTER L and CAMPBELL JAMES B carrier of T-0700 — a token the two records share that a namesake would have to share as well. He was corporation counsel and then clerk and collector across the municipal year, so the man was in the town at the October 1833 auction.

Two school-section parcels at the October 1833 auction. The town holds one Clybourne and so does the register; Andreas's roster gives the trade, butcher, and explains in the same clause why the household's division is outside_town — he lived north of the limits and could not vote in the village. A family assessed in the county since the 1820s and named on the town's own rolls in 1833 is not a stranger the surname happened to match.

All three tokens agree, which is exactly what carried FRAME DAVID P in T-0700. The register prints COLE PARKER M; the Chicago Democrat's letter list of 9 July 1834 prints 'Parker M. Cole'. The card began as a letter-list identity, and under this file's own rule that would refuse it — but the clause refuses a BARE name read once off a letter list, and this one is not bare: the middle initial is printed by the post office and by the land office alike, and the town's rolls and three later directories hold the man after. The register holds one Cole.

A documented tavern keeper at Wolf Point, printed by name in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 and keeping the house that was the district polling place on 9 December 1833 — the town has him in residence in the weeks around the 24 October 1833 school-section parcel, and again in June 1835 for the federal entry in T39N R13E. One Ingersoll in the register, one in the layer, and the forename agrees in full.

Two school-section parcels of October 1833. The town holds one Lloyd and the register holds one; beyond the name there are two independent documents around the entry — a contemporary Chicago paper naming him in the town, and Norris's directory of 1844 naming him still there eleven years after the auction. Two documents on the town's side is what this file's rule asks for where there is no initial and no trade to check.

Four rows, the forename in full, one Pruyne in the register and one in the layer. Andreas and the history of medicine in Chicago both hold him as a druggist in the town, and Fergus 1839 prints him at the city election of 1837 — so the town's record spans the 1833 auction and the 1835 federal entry alike.

An initial alone would not carry it. What carries it is the PEARSONS H argument: the SAME register spells this purchaser PRUYNE PETER on four other rows, one of them at the same auction two days earlier, and the town holds no second Pruyne for the initial to belong to. The single school-section parcel of 25 October 1833 is the same hand the register writes out in full elsewhere.

Refused for the reason T-0700 refused GARRETT A ET CO, and the reason is the register's own words: 'AND CO' is the page saying the buyer was a PARTNERSHIP. This crosswalk proposes a correspondence between a purchaser and a PERSON, so a card that says Peter Pruyne entered this parcel says something the page does not — the house entered it. That the house was his is likely and is not what is refused. Reading firms as entities in their own right is T-0851.

Eleven federal entries and 1,360 acres between 26 June and 16 October 1835, the largest single block in this cohort. The town's tax list of 1833 names a Jeremiah Price, and Fergus 1839, Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 all hold him after — four documents beyond the register, spanning the year of the purchases on both sides. The register spells the surname one way only and the layer holds one Price.

Three school-section parcels on 22 October 1833. The town's own polls of 1834 and 1835 both print 'Steele, Ashbel', Andreas gives the trade, plasterer, and neither register nor layer holds a second Steele. An unusual forename printed identically by the land office and by the town's clerk is a token, not a coincidence of surname.

The register's own Residence column, which is the strongest thing this source ever offers and what carried DILL FRANK in T-0700: three of these four rows state COOK. A man of this name was of Cook County when he entered 320 acres in October and December 1834, and a contemporary Chicago paper names John Ludby in the town on 19 November 1834, between the two entries. Fergus 1839 and 1843 hold him after. One Ludby in the register, one in the layer.

The card is a letter-list identity, which this file's rule refuses where the name is bare — and this one is not bare. The Democrat's return of 2 July 1834 prints 'Henry c. West' and the register prints WEST HENRY C: the middle initial is on both sides, which is exactly the FRAME DAVID P ruling of T-0700 and exactly what SPENCER WILLIAM G lacked when it was refused, its initial being one the town had never seen. West is a common surname and the initial is what narrows it; without that token this would be refused with the other letter-list four.

One canal entry of 29 September 1830, and on the town's side one line of the 1833 tax list and nothing else — a G3 identity, read once and corroborated by nothing. Two bare names three years apart, and no initial, trade, or second document between them. The residence column reads ILLINOIS, which is a state and does not reach the town. The proposal rests on the residents layer holding exactly one Hartzell, which is a fact about the layer and not about these two records agreeing. A second reading naming him — a deed, a directory, a paper — would overturn it.

Five school-section parcels on 24 October 1833, and on the town's side a single line of the 1833 tax list — G3, read once, corroborated by nothing. The surname is unique in both the register and the layer, and that is the whole of the case: rarity makes the coincidence unlikely, and unlikely is not checked. Nothing on the card can be put against the page — no initial, no trade, no second document, and a residence column reading UNKNOWN on all five rows. Refused with Hartzell and Vanderbogert as one class: one bare-name reading on each side.

Twenty-six school-section parcels, and the register's own pages are what refuse this. HALE EBENEZER enters every one of those parcels as well — the twenty-six duplicate entries T-0885 filed, two names on one parcel on one day on one page of volume 818 — and whether that pair is one transaction or two is a question this project has explicitly left open with the evidence beside it. Against that, the town's side holds one newspaper reading of a very common forename and surname, with no initial and no trade. Writing twenty-six purchases onto John Hale's card would decide T-0885 by default, in the direction that flatters the reconstruction. Refused until it is decided.

The town's man is James C Spence and the register prints SPENCE JAMES — no middle initial at all. So the one token that could be checked sits on the town's side only, which is the mirror of the SPENCER WILLIAM G refusal and fails for the same reason: an initial that appears on one record and not the other tests nothing. Behind the name the card is G2a, the 1835 poll list alone, and the poll's own bound falls after the scene date. Four rows over two years against a bare James Spence is not enough.

One school-section parcel of four acres, 24 October 1833. The town knows this person from ONE return of uncalled-for letters, printed 'Joveph Chandler' in the Democrat of 8 April 1834 — six months AFTER the entry — and the corroboration that lifted the card is a 'J. Chandler' at the city election of May 1837, which the card itself says is evidence of continued residence and not of anything in 1833. Neither offers a token to check the register against, and Joseph Chandler is a common name. This is the clause T-0700 wrote for SPENCER and WILSON.

Five school-section parcels for $663, and on the town's side one return of uncalled-for letters — printed 'Paul Kingston “74.1' in the Democrat of 1 April 1834, six months after the auction — plus later research rows that corroborate the person without printing anything the register can be put against. The register also holds KINGSTON J T and KINGSTON JOHN T, so the surname is not singling this buyer out on the page either. A correspondent believing a name reachable at Chicago and a name entering five parcels are two bare names.

The closest call in this cohort, and it goes the same way. The Democrat's letter list of 20 May 1835 prints 'Minard, Ira 2'; the register enters an Ira Minard on 161 acres in T40N R14E five weeks later, on 27 June 1835. The proximity is striking and it is not a check: the card is a letter-list identity with nothing else on it, no initial, no trade, no second document, and the residence column reads UNKNOWN on both rows. Upholding here would be upholding a coincidence of date, which is the register telling us when somebody bought, not who. One further reading naming Ira Minard in the town would carry it.

T-0700 refused GARRETT A ET CO as a firm and expected this spelling to stand alone on the card. It does not stand. The town has never read this man's forename: the corpus prints 'A. Garrett' — and, garbled, 'A. Gatren' and 'GARRETT' — in four numbers of the American and the Democrat, and an initial is LESS than the bare name the refusal clause was written for. The register offers Augustus, which is a full forename the town cannot check against anything it holds; that is the SPENCER WILLIAM G shape exactly. The trade does not rescue it either: an auctioneer is consistent with any land transaction whatever, which is what makes it useless as a discriminator, unlike the register of the land office that carried WHITLOCK JAMES. So A. Garrett's card carries no land purchase at all, and that is the honest state of it. One printing of the forename in full — a directory line, a deed, an advertisement signed out — would overturn this at once.

UPHELD on the middle name, which the town prints in full and the register prints three ways. The card reads F Gantry Blanchard because the town's own directories print him so: Fergus 1843 has 'Blanchard, Francis Gurtrey, capitalist, res 45 Wells', Fergus 1839 'Blanchard, Francis G., real estate dealer, Lake street', Norris 1844 'Blanchard, Francis G.' — one man, forename Francis, middle name Gurtrey, which is the token this card carries as Gantry. The register spells the same man BLANCHARD F G, BLANCHARD F G AS, BLANCHARD FRANCIS G and BLANCHARD GURTREY, and every one of those is a reading of Francis Gurtrey. So the initial that fired the mechanical rule is not what carries the ruling: what carries it is a middle name the town prints out loud and the register repeats, on a surname the layer holds three of. The trade agrees too — a real estate dealer of 1839 is what a man who bought school-section town lots in the sale of October 1833 becomes, and that is a consistency rather than a proof. THE THING THIS RULING DOES NOT DECIDE: the residents layer holds a SECOND card, Gantry Blanchard, and on this reading the two are very likely one man. That is a duplicate-card question, filed as T-0993 beside T-0844's cluster of six; this ruling rules only that the register's F G is the card the crosswalk named.

UPHELD on the middle name, which the town prints in full and the register prints three ways. The card reads F Gantry Blanchard because the town's own directories print him so: Fergus 1843 has 'Blanchard, Francis Gurtrey, capitalist, res 45 Wells', Fergus 1839 'Blanchard, Francis G., real estate dealer, Lake street', Norris 1844 'Blanchard, Francis G.' — one man, forename Francis, middle name Gurtrey, which is the token this card carries as Gantry. That is a duplicate-card question, filed as T-0993 beside T-0844's cluster of six; this ruling rules only that the register's F G is the card the crosswalk named. This spelling is the same day and the same block as ls0073 — lot 2 of block 26 against lot 7 — and the trailing AS is the register's own token, carried as the clerk wrote it and not read as part of a name.

UPHELD on the middle name, which the town prints in full and the register prints three ways. The card reads F Gantry Blanchard because the town's own directories print him so: Fergus 1843 has 'Blanchard, Francis Gurtrey, capitalist, res 45 Wells', Fergus 1839 'Blanchard, Francis G., real estate dealer, Lake street', Norris 1844 'Blanchard, Francis G.' — one man, forename Francis, middle name Gurtrey, which is the token this card carries as Gantry. The register spells the same man BLANCHARD F G, BLANCHARD F G AS, BLANCHARD FRANCIS G and BLANCHARD GURTREY, and every one of those is a reading of Francis Gurtrey. So the initial that fired the mechanical rule is not what carries the ruling: what carries it is a middle name the town prints out loud and the register repeats, on a surname the layer holds three of. The trade agrees too — a real estate dealer of 1839 is what a man who bought school-section town lots in the sale of October 1833 becomes, and that is a consistency rather than a proof. THE THING THIS RULING DOES NOT DECIDE: the residents layer holds a SECOND card, Gantry Blanchard, and on this reading the two are very likely one man. That is a duplicate-card question, filed as T-0993 beside T-0844's cluster of six; this ruling rules only that the register's F G is the card the crosswalk named. Here the register prints the forename in full, Francis, which is the word Fergus 1839 and Norris 1844 print; the abbreviation is on the town's side of this pair, not the register's.

UPHELD on a forename too odd to be a coincidence of initials, printed on both sides. The card reads S. Foot because the Democrat prints '§. FOOT' and Norris 1844 'Foot, S. teamster' — but Fergus 1839 and 1843 print the word itself: 'Foot, Star, teamster' and 'Foot, Starr, teamster, 180 Clark, cor Monroe'. The register's STAN is a fifth reading of Star/Starr, one letter apart in a transcription-mediated deposit, and not a fourth Christian name beginning with S. That is a token beyond the bare initial and it is what carries the ruling. The register's own arrangement agrees: the two Foots it holds, FOOT JOHN and FOOT STAN, take four consecutive lots of block 117 on one day, 22 October 1833 — John lots 5 and 6, Stan lots 3 and 4 — and the residents layer independently holds exactly two Foots, John and this one. THE LATER DIRECTORIES ARE USED HERE FOR THE NAME AND NOTHING ELSE: 'teamster' is a trade of 1839 and is not back-projected onto 1835, and the card's 1835 trade stays the paper's.

REFUSED against C Goodrich. The town's whole record of that person is one line of the 1833 tax list — an initial and a surname, no trade, no street, no second document, no directory entry in 1839, 1843 or 1844 — and the card says so itself: a projected resident, documented once and corroborated by nothing else, the weakest rung of the ratified ladder. The register prints CHAUNCEY, a forename the town has never seen, and there is nothing on the town's side for it to be checked against. The mechanical rule reached this card because the initial C picked it out of the three Goodriches the layer holds, which is a fact about the layer and not about the man. That both records put a Goodrich at Chicago in 1833 does not close the gap: the school-section sale of October 1833 and the tax list of the same year are the two places a Chicago Goodrich would appear whether or not he is the same Goodrich. Four rows are retracted — lot 4 of block 48 and blocks 130, 131 and 132, $489 of ground.

UPHELD, and the register settles it without leaving the deposit. The same register prints HADDOCK EDWARD H twice — ls0172, lot 7 of block 120, 25 October 1833, three days after the E H rows and inside the same school-section sale, and ls0669 in the country in 1835 — so the abbreviation and the full forename are one hand at one sale. The middle initial H stands on both sides: the town prints 'Haddock, Edward H., commission merchant, South Water st' in Fergus 1839 and John Wentworth's old-settler roll in the Tribune of 25 April 1882 carries 'Edward H. Haddock'. The card is the layer's strongest kind — seven sources, Andreas, the 1840 census, the Democrat — and the layer's only other Haddock is an H Haddock the forename refuses. Nothing here regrades the card or asserts a residence: it was already a documented townsman, and what the ruling adds is that these three rows are his.

UPHELD on the middle initial, which a contemporary Chicago paper prints and the register repeats. The Democrat of 31 December 1833, column 2, names him 'J. W. REED.' and gives his trade as cabinet maker — that is the town's own record, not a later directory — and the register prints REED JAMES W. Two tokens agree, not one: the W refuses George, Thomas and William Reed, and the forename refuses S W Reed, who is the only other Reed in the layer carrying a W. The register's other Reeds are ROBERT and THOMAS, and it never spells this purchaser any other way. The three lots are one day, 25 October 1833, inside the school-section sale. The household this person sits on is a reconstructed roof raised by the occupation census and this ruling does not touch it: it rules on the man, not the dwelling.

UPHELD, and like Haddock the register expands its own abbreviation: WRIGHT TRUMAN G appears twice in the same deposit, ls0518 and ls0566, both 27 June 1835 in T40N R14E. The middle initial G is on both sides — the card reads Truman G Wright off the tax list of 1833, the poll of 1834, a letter list and the old-settler death notices — and it is what refuses the five other Wrights the layer holds, of whom three are Johns. The trade agrees in the strongest way this domain allows: Fergus 1839 prints 'Wright, Truman G., speculator, bds Tremont House', and six lots and blocks taken in block 70 and around it over three days of the October 1833 school-section sale — $1,282 of town ground in one week — is a speculator at work and not a householder buying somewhere to live. The word speculator is 1839's and is not written onto the 1835 card; it is used here to check an identity, which is what this file is for.

UPHELD on the initials as the town itself prints them, and on a date only one Beaubien can reach. The town's record of this man does not hold a forename it has to have expanded for it: Andreas's 1833 roster prints 'J. B. Beaubien, merchant' and Fergus 1839 prints 'Beaubien, John B., Michigan ave., bet. Lake and So. Water sts' — J. B. is the form the town used, and the register's BEAUBIEN J B is that form. The layer holds ten Beaubiens and the sale is dated 29 September 1830: this card's arrival is attested at 1812 from Andreas — 'he came to Chicago and bought the cabin and cultivated field south of the old fort in 1812' — and it is the only Beaubien in the layer the record puts at Chicago that early. Four canal rows in section 29 of T39N R14E, two of them the register's own voided duplicates of the other two, carried at 212.61 acres and $1,063.20 net. TWO THINGS THIS DOES NOT DO: it does not touch the Fort Dearborn reservation claim, which this project holds no record of and makes no finding on, and it does not make the 1830 purchase evidence of residence — the Residence column reads ILLINOIS on the voided pair and UNKNOWN on the pair that stood, and neither names a town.

REFUSED against L W Smith, on the same ground as SPENCER WILLIAM G under T-0700. The town's whole record of L W Smith is one line of the poll of 1834 — the card calls itself a projected resident, documented once and corroborated by nothing else — with no trade, no street, no second document and no entry in any of the three directories. The register offers LIMAN, and the very next row, ls0573, offers SIMAN for the same tract on the same day at a price one cent apart: the deposit itself does not know whether the man was a Lyman or a Simon, so the token the mechanical rule matched on is not stable in the source that supplies it. The register's row carries no middle initial at all, so the W — the one token that could discriminate among the eleven Smiths the layer holds — is checked against nothing. The COOK in the Residence column sits on the SIMAN reading, not this one, and Cook County in 1834 reaches far beyond the town. One row retracted, 140.18 acres in T38N R14E section 2.

UPHELD, and this is the cleanest in the cohort: the register's forename is the town's own printed forename. Fergus 1843 has 'Montgomery, Loton W., shoemaker, Jerome Beecher, res Market', and the register prints MONTGOMERY LOTON WM and MONTGOMERY LOTON W — Loton is not a name the deposit could have arrived at from an initial. The 1835 card itself rests on the Democrat, which prints 'L. W. MONTGOMERY' in five issues between 17 December 1833 and 20 May 1835 and gives the trade as boot and shoe maker, so the middle initial W is contemporary and not borrowed from 1843. The layer's only other Montgomery is a W Montgomery the forename refuses, and the register's only other is a JOHN whose Residence reads MCLEAN. Eighty acres of the east half of the south-east quarter of section 22, T38N R14E, on 24 November 1835 — the land rush, well south of the town, and the ruling asserts nothing about where he lived.

UPHELD on the same ground as MONTGOMERY LOTON WM: Fergus 1843's 'Montgomery, Loton W., shoemaker' is the register's forename printed by the town, and the Democrat carries L. W. Montgomery through five issues of 1833–1835 with the trade. This is the earlier of his two entries — the north-west quarter of section 23, T38N R14E, 160 acres at $200 on 27 June 1835 — and it sits five months before and one section east of the other, which is one man buying twice in the rush rather than two readings of one sale.

REFUSED against T. M. Morrison, and refused on the rule's own named case. The town holds nothing but 'Morrison, T. M.' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office, the Democrat of 20 May 1835, column 13 — no trade, no street, no household, no directory entry — and an uncalled-for letter says only that a correspondent thought the name reachable at Chicago. The M does appear on both sides, and that is the argument for upholding it; it does not carry, because the M is not a second reading of the man, it is one more character of the same single line, printed by the same list that supplies the T. The register adds THOS, which the town has never seen, and the layer holds five Morrisons — one of them Orsemus Morrison, a documented townsman who bought three town lots at the school-section sale, which is what a Morrison in this register looks like when the town really knows him. The ground here is a fractional quarter in T38N R15E section 32, the far south-east corner of the ring, 78.94 acres, and one row is retracted.

UPHELD, and the register proves it against itself. ls0919 — HUNTER E E, the north-east quarter of section 13, T40N R13E, 80 acres, $100, 15 November 1834 — and ls0920 — HUNTER EDWARD E, the same quarter of the same section on the same day at the same price — are one entry read twice, and the fuller reading states COOK in the Residence column where the abbreviated one leaves it UNKNOWN. So the expansion of E E to EDWARD E is the deposit's, not this ruling's, and it comes with the one column that speaks to residence. The middle initial E is on the town's side as well: the card is attested at G1b off the Democrat, the poll of 1834 and the old-settler death notices, and Fergus 1839 prints him as deputy-sheriff and ex-justice of the peace on Wells street. The layer's four other Hunters are refused on the forename. COOK is a county and not a town, and this ruling reads it as the register's word for the county, exactly as the domain's grading rule does.

withdrawn.reasoning: One school-section parcel; on the town's side one line of the 1833 tax list and nothing else. Two things make the refusal firmer than the thinness alone. The register itself holds a SECOND man of this surname — VANDERBOGERT JOHN AS, an assignment — so the surname does not single anyone out even on the page. And the town's own spelling of this family is under an open question: T-0842 asks whether Van Den Bogart and Van der Bogart are one man printed two ways or two men, with a card minted for the second. Ruling an identity onto a name whose identity is itself the open ticket is the order this project does not work in.
withdrawn.withdrawn_why: NOT REVERSED — LEFT WITHOUT A PROPOSAL TO RULE ON. T-0842 ruled the Van der Bogart cluster on 2026-09-10 and folded the town's card `vanderbogert_henry` (the 1833 tax list's 'Vanderbogert, Henry') onto `vanderbogart_henry`, Dr Henry Van der Bogart. The mechanical rule in build_resident_crosswalk() keys on the surname EXACTLY, so with no `Vanderbogert` left in the residents layer it now refuses both of the register's rows on 'the residents layer holds nobody of the surname' and proposes nothing — and a ruling on a proposal that was never made is what --check calls a ruling on nothing. The reasoning is kept here whole rather than deleted, because it is still the answer if the proposal comes back. WHAT T-0842 CHANGED ABOUT ITS SUBSTANCE, honestly: one of the refusal's two stated grounds is gone — the town's spelling of this family is no longer an open question — and the town's side is no longer 'one line of the 1833 tax list and nothing else' but an attested man with four readings behind him. The other ground stands untouched: the register itself holds VANDERBOGERT JOHN AS as well, so the surname still does not single a purchaser out on the register's own page. This entry does NOT re-rule it either way. The crosswalk's exact-surname key is the thing to fix first, and that is filed as its own ticket.

withdrawn_doc: Rulings whose proposal the crosswalk no longer makes. --check reads `ruled` only, and refuses a ruling on a proposal that was never made; a judgement is still worth keeping when the proposal under it moves, so it is parked here with the reason and the day. Restore a row to `ruled` if and when the crosswalk proposes it again — and read the withdrawal note first, because what the town holds may have changed under it.
